winner.title: Dambou: the Nigerien recipe with millet couscous and moringa leaves
winner.source: NKOSI (commercial African-food brand blog, Equipe NKOSI)

evidence.authenticity: Names Zarma and Songhai origin, millet couscous steamed, then mixed with boiled leaves, onion, chili; but main leaf is spinach with moringa as the alternate, uses stock cube, and the author is a brand team, not a Nigerien cook.
evidence.precision: Grams for 2 of 8 ingredients (400 g couscous, 250 g leaves); 10 cl oil; 'tender' cue on steaming; no temps, no pan sizes; onion and chili unsized.
evidence.testing: No sign of testing and no explanation of why; short origin blurb only.
evidence.photos: 0 step images in schema; 57 images on page are likely site chrome and products.
evidence.efficiency: 45 minutes total, no wasted steps; leaves boil while couscous steams.
evidence.access: Millet couscous needs an African grocery or online order and has no sub; spinach and dried moringa are offered as options.

winner.why: It is the only candidate that is actually Nigerien dambou with weights, beating the Hausa rice variant from Nigeria (BusinessDay) on authenticity and precision, though it still falls short of 60.

runnerUp.title: Dambun Shinkafa, a Northern Nigerian rice dish
runnerUp.source: BusinessDay (Lehle Balde; recipe by chef Halima Zawiya, Kano)

evidence.authenticity: Hausa dambun shinkafa from Nigeria by a Kano chef; rice grits with moringa, a related regional variant rather than the Zarma millet dambou.
evidence.precision: Cup measures for most items, a big bowl of moringa, no weights; cues only 'half-cooked' then 'completely cooked'; Maggi cube unquantified.
evidence.testing: Some reasoning: broken rice softens best, moringa on the rack prevents overcooking; no testing.
evidence.access: Rice grits, atarugu peppers, and zogale have no subs given.

runnerUp.why: A newspaper feature with cup measures and little cue detail, and a Hausa rice variant, so it ranks below NKOSI.
